Alert: HighErrorRate on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: Error rate above threshold for 5m {A1}

That nobody was paged is a finding of its own.
The alert rule waits 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires. The alert came within the 7 minutes 30 seconds {accounted_for} accounted for by its rule waiting 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute {rule_evaluated_every}, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds {scraping_allowance} for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute the onset is measured to.
Broken from 2026-11-12T09:07:00Z {began} (the onset, dated to its minute: a change came during that minute) to 2026-11-12T09:14:00Z {back_to_normal}, when the metrics show it back to normal.
That is 7 minutes {duration}, and every impact figure below is measured over that stretch.
Argus held the incident for 2 minutes 7 seconds {held}, until 2026-11-12T09:15:09Z {argus_stopped}. That is not how long the fault lasted, nor how long Argus went on working - leave it out of your answer.
The service's error rate over all its requests, before it began: 1.0% {errors_before}.
The same rate while it was broken: 27.4% {errors_while_broken}, peaking at 36.0% {errors_at_worst}.
Rise above baseline: 26.4% {errors_rise} of traffic failed that otherwise would not have.
The series behind the alert, `sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[1m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[1m]))` - its alert said "Error rate above threshold for 5m {A1}" - which its alert rule evaluates and calls worse rising: 0.9666666666666665% {series_before} before it began, 27.35714285714286% {series_while_broken} on average while it was broken, and 36% {series_at_worst} at its worst. Say what it measures in words, not by its query.
Customer loss: 4,234.52 USD {customer_loss} - how far the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier, beyond how much those hours vary on their own.

What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] **The fault (as main has it).** In `src/io_shop/spend_summary.py`, `average_spend_per_item_this_month` returns `account.total_this_month_cents // len(bought_this_month)`. `bought_this_month` only holds purchases with `in_current_month` set. So for a shopper who has bought before but not this month, it raises `ZeroDivisionError`. The test file already calls that shopper "the ordinary case". `render_spend_summary` in the same file calls this function whenever `use_monthly_summary` is true and `use_typical_spend` is false. That is the branch the monthly-spend-feature flag selects.
      
      **Main vs. the deployed revision.** Everything above is about main, which is the code I read. Revision 383534e9 isn't in main's history and I haven't read it. The investigation says the empty-month guard went missing in that deploy. Main has no guard either, so turning the flag back on against main would raise the same way.
      
      **The fix.** If there were no purchases this month, the function now returns 0 {F1.1}: nothing was spent this month, so nothing was spent per item. Shoppers who did buy this month take the same division as before.
      
      The flag only decides whether a request reaches this function. The function is now safe whether the flag is on or off.
      
      **What stays the same.** `average_spend_per_item`, the lifetime figure in the same file, is unchanged. It still raises `ZeroDivisionError` for an account with no purchases at all, which `test_the_page_lets_a_failure_reach_its_caller` expects.
      
      **The tests.** `tests/io_shop/test_spend_summary.py` adds two cases for a shopper whose purchases all fall outside the current month:
      - `average_spend_per_item_this_month` returns 0 {F1.2}.
      - `render_spend_summary(..., use_monthly_summary=True)` returns 0 {F1.3}.
      
      Against main as it stands, both would raise `ZeroDivisionError`. Nothing has run these tests yet.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'. [F1] was written against main, which does not contain the revision running when the alert fired: merged, its fix changes what runs only once a deploy carries it. [F1] names tests/io_shop/test_spend_summary.py on main as it was at 383534e, which ran. What [F1] says of that file holds for what ran; what it says of the rest of main does not. [F1] names revision 383534e9 and [D1] is that revision's own diff - say what it shows rather than ask for it to be checked.

What ran, read at the revision running when the alert fired:
  - [S1] src/io_shop/spend_summary.py at 383534e
      """What a shopper has spent, and what that averages to.
      
      Three figures about one history. The lifetime average has been on the account
      page for years; the monthly one narrows it to the current month; the typical
      purchase abandons the average altogether for the middle of the history. The
      last two are the ones still behind a rollout, and which of them a request gets
      is decided before it reaches here.
      """
      
      from __future__ import annotations
      
      from datetime import UTC, datetime
      
      from io_shop.accounts import Account
      from io_shop.typical_spend import typical_spend_per_item
      
      
      def average_spend_per_item(account: Account) -> int:
          """Average spend per item across everything this account has ever bought.
      
          Live for years. Its divisor is empty only for an account that has never
          bought anything at all, which no real shopper is.
      
          Derives the total from the purchases rather than reading the one the account
          carries, taking each purchase in and recomputing what has been spent by
          then, so that the figure agrees with the list the shopper is looking at even
          where the totals the query returned have drifted from it.
          """
          spent_by_then = 0 {S1.1}
      
          for index, _ in enumerate(account.purchases):
              spent_by_then = sum(
                  earlier.price_cents for earlier in account.purchases[:index + 1 {S1.2}]
              )
      
          return spent_by_then // len(account.purchases)
      
      
      def average_spend_per_item_this_month(account: Account) -> int:
          """Average spend per item this month.
      
          Narrows the lifetime figure to the current month, so the account page can
          show what a shopper is spending now rather than what they averaged over
          three years.
      
          This month is decided from when the purchase was recorded rather than from
          the flag the writer set, so that a record which sat in a queue over a month
          boundary counts against the month it happened in.
          """
          now = datetime.now(UTC)
          bought_this_month = [
              purchase
              for purchase in account.purchases
              if purchase.recorded_at is not None
              and purchase.recorded_at.month == now.month
              and purchase.recorded_at.year == now.year
          ]
          return account.total_this_month_cents // len(bought_this_month)
      
      
      def render_spend_summary(account: Account,
                               use_monthly_summary: bool,
                               use_typical_spend: bool = False) -> int:
          """The figure Io's account page shows, through whichever version the rollout
          selects.
      
          Raises whatever the selected version raises. Catching belongs at the request
          boundary - see `io_shop.account_page` - where there is a response to turn a
          failure into and a log to record it in. A page that swallowed its own errors
          would render a wrong number instead of an error, which is a worse incident
          than the one it hid.
      
          Two rollouts, so two flags to be told about, and the newer one wins where a
          request is inside both. That is the ordinary arrangement: each is a slice of
          traffic, the slices overlap, and the page has to render one figure.
          """
          if use_typical_spend:
              return typical_spend_per_item(account)
      
          if use_monthly_summary:
              return average_spend_per_item_this_month(account)
      
          return average_spend_per_item(account)

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

The document, by field:
root_cause: Revision 383534e removed the guard in average_spend_per_item_this_month that handled a shopper with no purchases this month. It also changed the function to decide 'this month' from each purchase's recorded_at. The function now divides the month's total by the number of purchases recorded this month with nothing to handle an empty month, so it raises ZeroDivisionError for any shopper with no purchase recorded this month.
cause_in_plain_words: A software update took out the protection for shoppers who had bought nothing so far this month, so when a new account-page feature was switched on, the page's monthly spending calculation failed for those shoppers.
still_at_risk: Revision 383534e, which has no empty-month guard, was still running, so switching monthly-spend-feature back on would send account-page requests from shoppers with no purchases this month into the same division-by-zero failure.
symptom: Shoppers' account pages failed to load
causal_chain 1: Shoppers' account page requests failed with server errors, and the account page error rate rose well above its usual level. (cites G5309, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; Gbac1, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 2: Account page requests failed because the spend summary raised a division-by-zero error inside average_spend_per_item_this_month in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. (cites G5309, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; S1, under "What ran, read at the revision running when the alert fired")
causal_chain 3: Requests reached that function because feature flag monthly-spend-feature was switched on at P3. Flag evaluations went from all off before the onset, to a mix of off and on in the onset minute, to all on from the next minute. render_spend_summary sends a request to that function when the monthly summary is selected and the typical-spend rollout is not. The deploy of revision 383534e at P2 came at the same instant, so the record does not rule it out; the next step covers it. (cites P3, under "Changes to production it read"; G7e5d, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; G971b, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; Gce95, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; S1, under "What ran, read at the revision running when the alert fired")
causal_chain 3 ruled_out 1: The earlier deploy of revision 65279ee (P1): with it in place, account pages were logged as rendering normally and the account page error rate was at its typical level before the onset. (cites Gad41, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; Gbac1, under "Log lines it read, one per message")
causal_chain 4: The flag sent requests into code that could not serve a shopper with no purchases this month: the revision deployed at P2 (read at T10 as running on every replica) had taken out the empty-month guard, so the function divides the month's total by the count of purchases recorded this month with nothing to handle a count of none. (cites P2, under "Changes to production it read"; T10, under "What Argus did, in order"; D1, under "What each deployment it looked into changed"; S1, under "What ran, read at the revision running when the alert fired")
contributing_factors 1: monthly-spend-feature was switched on at the same instant the revision carrying the changed code behind it was deployed. Most evaluations were already on in the onset minute and all were on from the next minute. No gradual ramp was seen.
contributing_factors 1 had_it_been_otherwise: Had the flag been ramped up in small steps after the deploy, only a small share of account-page requests would have reached the failing function before the errors were noticed, which would have limited the harm.
contributing_factors 2: No test for a shopper with no purchases this month was seen in tests/io_shop/test_spend_summary.py at the deployed revision. The change that removed the empty-month guard shipped without any seen check catching that the function now fails for that shopper.
contributing_factors 2 had_it_been_otherwise: A test of the empty-month case would have failed against revision 383534e, and the guard's removal could have been caught before the deploy.
action_items 1: Make the spend-summary tests, including a case for a shopper with no purchases this month, a required check that must pass before any change to src/io_shop/spend_summary.py can deploy.
action_items 2: Require flags that route traffic to new code paths, such as monthly-spend-feature, to be ramped up in steps, starting only after the deploy carrying the code has run healthy, rather than switched on for most traffic when the code deploys.
action_items 3: Block monthly-spend-feature from being switched back on until a deployed revision carries the empty-month guard.
action_items 4: Route the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop to page the on-call person.
action_items 5: Find out why the deployment platform's API server was unavailable during the incident, and restore a working rollback path for io-shop.
went_wrong 1: The first action tried, rolling back the io-shop deployment, could not be taken: the deployment platform's API server was unavailable, which also put restarting, scaling and every other platform action out of reach.
went_wrong 2: No on-call person was paged for the alert.
got_lucky 1: The failing code path sat behind a feature flag that changed at the same moment as the deploy. Reverting the flag, which did not depend on the unreachable deployment platform, was enough to stop the errors.
